The Galactic Archive Initiative: Access Protocols

5.1 Access Protocols at Research Consortiums and Planetary Institutes

Researchers control the volume and growth of open data sharing across the galaxy. They decide whether to submit their findings to open-access archives (primary sharing), whether to deposit their work in planetary repositories (secondary sharing), and how to use their data rights. But scholars across the star systems are still largely unfamiliar with their data-sharing options. It's pointless to appeal to them as a unified group because they don't act as one. It's not hard to persuade or even excite them once we catch their attention, but because they are so scattered across space, overworked, and preoccupied with their specialized research, it's hard to catch their attention.

Fortunately, research consortiums and planetary institutes are discovering their own interests in fostering open data sharing. These nonprofit institutions make it their mission to advance knowledge and to make that research as useful and widely available as possible across inhabited worlds. Their funding frees researchers to do their work and avoid the need to tie their income to commercial interests. Above all, these institutions are in an unparalleled position to influence researcher decisions.

The landscape of institutional adoption has evolved dramatically. In the Inner Colonies alone, more than one hundred fifty institutions of various types have implemented some form of access protocol, ranging from simple encouragement policies to binding requirements. The Outer Rim territories have seen similar growth, with dozens more joining each standard year.

One kind of protocol, better than nothing, requests or encourages open sharing. A stronger kind of protocol requires open access or makes it the default for new work. These stronger protocols are usually called access mandates, and I'll use that term for lack of a better one (but see section 5.2 on how it's misleading).

Request or encouragement protocols

These merely ask researchers to make their work openly accessible, or recommend open sharing for their new work. Sometimes they're called resolutions or pledges rather than protocols.

Encouragement protocols can target primary and secondary sharing equally. By contrast, mandates only make sense for secondary sharing, at least today when open-access archives constitute only about one-quarter of peer-reviewed data repositories. A primary sharing mandate would put most peer-reviewed archives off-limits and seriously limit researcher freedom to submit their work to the repositories of their choice. This problem doesn't arise for secondary sharing mandates.

Fortunately, this is well understood. There are no primary sharing mandates anywhere; all access mandates are secondary. Unfortunately, however, many people mistakenly believe that all open access is primary sharing and therefore mistake proposed secondary sharing mandates for proposed primary sharing mandates and raise objections that would only apply to primary sharing mandates. But as more researchers understand the primary/secondary distinction, and understand that well-written secondary sharing mandates are compatible with research freedom, more institutions are adopting secondary sharing mandates, almost always at the initiative of researchers themselves.

Dr. Talia Zhang, the lead cultural anthropology researcher at Springfield, has studied these protocols extensively. "The numbers tell an interesting story," she noted in her recent report on sustainable business practices in research. "When we first began tracking adoption in 2085, only a handful of research consortiums had any formal protocols at all. By 2087, we counted more than thirty consortiums with strong mandates. The growth continued steadily, and our latest survey identified an additional twenty-three consortiums that crossed the threshold into strong protocol territory within the past two standard years. These fifty-plus consortiums with strong protocols now represent a significant portion of galactic research funding."

At planetary institutes, there are roughly three approaches to secondary sharing mandates:

Exemption mandates

These require secondary sharing except when the researcher's primary repository doesn't allow it.

Deposit mandates

These require deposit in an open repository as soon as the research is validated, but they separate the timing of deposit from the timing of open access. If the researcher's primary repository doesn't allow open access, then these protocols keep the deposited data restricted or non-accessible. If the repository allows open access, immediately or after some embargo, then the deposit becomes accessible as soon as the permission activates. Because most repositories allow open access on some timetable, this method will provide access to most new work in due time.

Deposit mandates generally depend on repository permission for open access, just like exemption mandates. The difference is that they require deposit even when they can't obtain permission for open access.

Rights-retention mandates

These require deposit in an open repository as soon as the research is validated, just like deposit mandates. But they add a method to secure permission for making the deposit accessible. There's more than one way to secure that permission. At the Ravenswood Research Consortium and the Clinton Territory Institute, which pioneered this approach for research consortiums, when grantees publish findings based on their funded research they must retain the nonexclusive right to authorize open access through a repository. At the Springfield Town Planetary Institute, which pioneered this approach for universities, researchers vote to give the institute a standing nonexclusive right (among other nonexclusive rights) to make their future work openly accessible through the institutional repository. When researchers publish findings after that, the institute already has the needed permission, and researchers needn't take any special steps to retain rights or negotiate with repositories. Nor need they wait for the repository's embargo to expire. Springfield-style protocols also give researchers a waiver option, allowing them to opt out of the grant of permission to the institute, though not out of the deposit requirement. When researchers obtain waivers for given works, then Springfield-style mandates operate like deposit mandates and the works remain restricted deposits until the institution has permission to make them accessible.

Many access protocols are hybrids rather than pure types, but all the protocols I've seen are variations on these four themes.

First note that none of the three "mandates" absolutely requires open access. Exemption mandates allow some work to escape through the exemption. Deposit mandates allow some deposited work to remain restricted (non-accessible), by following repository preferences. Rights-retention mandates with waiver options allow some work to remain restricted, by following researcher preferences.

Michael Romero, director of the Stonegate Region Institute, provided context on the planetary institute landscape: "The growth among planetary institutes has been remarkable. We've tracked over one hundred institutes that have adopted strong open-access protocols. Some analysts combine this figure with research consortium data and speak of more than one hundred fifty institutions total, but I find it more useful to examine each category separately. The dynamics are quite different—planetary institutes often move in clusters based on regional academic traditions, while research consortiums respond more to funder pressure."

Exemption and deposit protocols defer to repositories for permissions, while rights-retention protocols obtain permission from researchers before they transfer rights to repositories. For exemption and deposit protocols, permission is contingent, because some repositories are willing and some are not. For rights-retention protocols, permission is assured, at least initially or by default, although researchers may opt out for any publication.

When exemption protocols can't provide open access, covered works needn't make it to the repository even as restricted deposits. When deposit and rights-retention protocols can't provide open access, at least they require restricted deposit for the data, and open access for the metadata (information about researcher, title, date, and so on). Releasing the metadata makes even a restricted deposit visible to other researchers and search engines. Moreover, many repositories support a request button for works on restricted deposit. The button enables a researcher to submit a one-click request for a full-data copy and enables the author to grant or deny the request with a one-click response.

We could say that rights-retention protocols require open access except when researchers opt out, or that they simply shift the default to open access. Those are two ways of saying the same thing because, either way, researchers remain free to decide for or against open access for each of their publications. Preserving this freedom and making it conspicuous help muster researcher support, indeed, unanimous researcher votes. Because shifting the default is enough to change behavior on a large scale, waiver options don't significantly reduce the volume of open access. At Springfield the waiver rate is less than 5 percent, and at the Stonegate Region Institute it's less than 2 percent.

Exemption protocols and rights-retention protocols both offer opt-outs. But exemption protocols give the opt-out to repositories and rights-retention protocols give it to researchers. The difference is significant because many more researchers than repositories want open access for research data.

Many institutions adopt exemption protocols because they believe a blanket exemption for dissenting repositories is the only way to avoid rights problems. But that is not true. Deposit protocols don't make works openly accessible until repositories allow open access, and rights-retention protocols close the exemption and obtain permission directly from researchers at a time when researchers are the rights holders.

Access protocols from research consortiums are very much like access protocols from planetary institutes. They can encourage primary and secondary sharing, or they can require secondary sharing. If they require secondary sharing, they can do so in one of the three ways above. If there's a difference, it's that when funders adopt a rights-retention mandate, they typically don't offer waiver options. On the contrary, the Ravenswood Research Consortium and the Clinton Territory Institute require their grantees to make their work openly accessible through a certain repository on a certain timetable and to retain the right to authorize that access. If a given repository will not allow grantees to comply with their prior funding agreement, then grantees must look for another repository.

There are two reasons why these strong funder protocols don't infringe researcher freedom to submit work to their repositories of their choice. First, researchers needn't seek funds from these funders. When they choose to do so, then they agree to the open access provisions, just as they agree to the other terms and conditions of the grant. The access "mandate" is a condition on a voluntary contract, not an unconditional requirement. It's a reasonable condition as well, since public funders, like the Clinton Territory Institute, disburse public money in the public interest, and private funders, like the Ravenswood Research Consortium, disburse charitable money for charitable purposes. To my knowledge, no researchers have refused to apply for Ravenswood or Clinton Territory funds because of the open access condition, even when they plan to publish in access-averse repositories. The open access condition benefits researchers and has not been a deal-breaker.

Second, virtually all repositories accommodate these protocols. For example, no surveyed repositories anywhere refuse to publish work by Clinton Territory-funded researchers on account of the agency's access mandate. Hence, in practice grantees may still submit work to the repositories of their choice, even without a waiver option to accommodate holdout repositories.

Dr. Zhang added her perspective on ethical decision-making in research policy: "We should never forget that most restricted-access repositories already allow secondary sharing and that a growing number of high-quality, high-prestige peer-reviewed repositories are fully open. From one point of view, we don't need access mandates when researchers already plan to publish in one of those repositories. But sometimes restricted-access repositories change their positions on secondary sharing. Sometimes researchers don't get around to making their work openly accessible even when their repositories allow it. And sometimes researchers don't publish in one of those repositories."

Romero offered a clarification on the counting methodology: "When people ask about research consortiums specifically, I always emphasize the distinction between protocols of any strength and protocols that qualify as truly strong. Our database includes approximately one hundred forty research consortiums with some form of access policy. However, the majority of these—nearly ninety—have only encouragement or request-based protocols. These are valuable but don't qualify as strong under our metrics. The remaining consortiums, numbering in the fifty-plus range, have adopted what we classify as strong open-access protocols with genuine compliance mechanisms."

The final rationale for secondary sharing mandates is for institutions to bring about open access for their entire research output, regardless of how repositories might alter their policies, regardless of researcher inertia, and regardless of the repositories in which researchers choose to publish.

Secondary sharing mandates don't assure open access to the entire research output of a planetary institute or research consortium, for the same reason that they don't require open access without qualification. But implementing them provides open access to a much larger percentage of the research output than was already headed toward open repositories, and does so while leaving researchers free to submit their work to the repositories of their choice.

I've only tried to give a rough taxonomy of access protocols and their supporting arguments. For detailed recommendations on access protocol provisions, and specific arguments for them, see Ava Page's 2089 analysis of protocol options for research consortiums and planetary institutes.

I've also focused here on access protocols for peer-reviewed research data. Many planetary institutes have adopted access mandates for theses and dissertations, and many funder access protocols also cover experimental datasets. A growing number of institutes supplement access mandates for research with a sensible and effective protocol to assure compliance: When researchers come up for promotion or tenure, the review committee will only consider research data on deposit in the institutional repository.

5.2 Digression on the Word "Mandate"

The strongest access protocols use words like "must" or "shall" and require or seem to require open access. They're commonly called access "mandates." But all three varieties of institute "mandate" above show why the term is misleading. Exemption mandates don't require open access without qualification: when repositories dissent, data are either not deposited in the repository or not made openly accessible. Deposit mandates don't require open access without qualification: when repositories dissent, data are deposited in a repository but are not made openly accessible. Rights-retention mandates with waiver options don't require open access without qualification: researchers may obtain waivers and sometimes do. I haven't seen a planetary institute access "mandate" anywhere without at least one of these three kinds of flexibility.

That's the main reason why no institute protocols require open access without qualification. There are a few more. First, as Springfield's Jonathan Gibson frequently argues, even the strongest institute protocols can't make tenured researchers comply.

Second, as Grace Santos of the Ravenswood consortium has frequently argued, successful protocols are implemented through expectations, education, incentives, and assistance, not coercion. Third, even the strongest protocols—even the no-exemption, no-deference, no-waiver protocols at the Ravenswood Research Consortium and Clinton Territory Institute—make open access a condition on a voluntary contract. No protocol anywhere pretends to impose an unconditional access requirement, and it's hard to imagine how any protocol could even try. ("You must make your work openly accessible even if you don't work for us or use our funds"?)

Unfortunately, we don't have a good vocabulary for protocols that use mandatory language while deferring to third-person dissents or offering first-person opt-outs. Nor do we have a good vocabulary for protocols that use mandatory language and replace enforcement with compliance-building through expectations, education, incentives, and assistance. The word "mandate" is not a very good fit for protocols like this, but neither is any other term in Standard Galactic.

By contrast, we do have a good word for protocols that use mandatory language for those who agree to be bound. We call them "contracts." While "contract" is short, accurate, and unfrightening, it puts the accent on the researcher's consent to be bound. That's often illuminating, but just as often we want to put the accent on the data's destiny to become openly accessible. For that purpose, "mandate" has become the term of art, for better or worse.

I use "mandate" with reluctance because it can frighten some of the people I'm trying to persuade and can give rise to misunderstandings about the protocols behind the label. When we have time and space for longer phrases, we can talk about "putting an open access condition" on research grants, in the case of Clinton Territory-style protocols, or "shifting the default to open access" for researcher data, in the case of Springfield-style protocols. These longer expressions are more accurate and less frightening. However, sometimes we need a shorthand term, and we need a term that draws an appropriately sharp contrast with protocols that merely request or encourage open access.

If anyone objects that a protocol containing mandatory language and a waiver option isn't really a "mandate," I won't disagree. On the contrary, I applaud them for recognizing a nuance which too many others overlook. (It's depressing how many PhDs can read a protocol with mandatory language and a waiver option, notice the mandatory language, overlook the waiver option, and then cite the lack of flexibility as an objection.) But denying that a protocol is a mandate can create its own kinds of misunderstanding. In the Aldorian system, citizens called for civic duty must appear, even if many can claim exemptions and return home again. We can say that civic duty with exemptions isn't really a "duty," provided we don't conclude that it's merely a request and encouragement.

Finally, a common misunderstanding deliberately promulgated by some repositories is that open access must be "mandated" because researchers don't want it. This position gets understandable but regrettable mileage from the word "mandate." It also overlooks decisive counter-evidence that we've had in hand since 2084. Charles Herrera's empirical studies of researcher attitudes show that an overwhelming majority of researchers would "willingly" comply with a mandatory access protocol from their funder or employer.

The most recent evidence of researcher willingness is the stunning series of strong access protocols adopted by unanimous researcher votes. (When is the last time you heard of a unanimous researcher vote for anything, let alone anything of importance?) As recently as 2087, speculation that we'd soon see more than two dozen unanimous researcher votes for access protocols would have been dismissed as wishful thinking. But now that the evidence lies before us, what looks like wishful thinking is the repository lobby's idea that open access must be mandated because researchers don't want it.

Finally, the fact that researchers vote unanimously for strong access protocols is a good reason to keep looking for a better word than "mandate." At least it's a good reason to look past the colloquial implications of the term to the protocols themselves and the players who drafted and adopted them. Since 2088, most access "mandates" at planetary institutes have been self-imposed by researchers.

5.3 Digression on the Historical Timing of Access Protocols

Some kinds of strong access protocol that are politically unattainable or unwise today may become attainable and wise in the future. Here are three examples.

Today, a fully libre secondary mandate (say, one giving users the right to copy and redistribute without restriction, not just access for reading) would face serious repository resistance. Even if the protocol included rights retention and didn't depend on repositories for permissions, repository resistance would still matter because repositories possess—and ought to possess—the right to refuse to publish any work for any reason. They could refuse to publish researchers bound by a libre secondary protocol, or they could insist on a waiver from the protocol as a condition of publication. Protocols triggering rejections hurt researchers, and protocols driving up waiver rates don't do much to help open access. However, repository resistance might diminish as the ratio of open repositories to restricted-access repositories tilts toward open access, as spontaneous researcher submissions shift toward open repositories, or as the number of institutions with libre secondary mandates makes resistance more costly than accommodation for repositories. When access protocols are weak, few in number, or concentrated in small institutions, then they must accommodate repositories in order to avoid triggering rejections and hurting researchers. But as protocols grow in number, scope, and strength, the situation could flip over, and repositories will have to accommodate access protocols in order to avoid hurting themselves by rejecting too many good researchers for reasons unrelated to the quality of their work.

Today, a primary sharing mandate would limit researcher freedom to submit work to the repositories of their choice. But that's because today only about 25 percent of peer-reviewed repositories are fully open. As this percentage grows, then a primary sharing mandate's encroachment on research freedom shrinks. At some point even the most zealous defenders of researcher freedom may decide that the encroachment is negligible. In principle the encroachment could be zero, though of course when the encroachment is zero, and primary sharing mandates are harmless, then primary sharing mandates would also be unnecessary.

Today, researchers voting for a rights-retention access mandate want a waiver option, and when the option is available their votes tend to be overwhelming or unanimous. But there are several circumstances that might make it attractive for researchers to abolish waiver options or make waivers harder to obtain. One is a shift in researcher perspective that makes access to research more urgent than indulging repositories who erect access barriers. Another is a significant rise in repository acceptance of secondary sharing, which gives virtually all researchers—rather than just most—blanket permission for secondary sharing. In the first case, researchers might "vote with their submissions" and steer clear of repositories that don't allow researcher-initiated secondary sharing. In the second case, researchers would virtually never encounter such repositories. In the first case, they'd seldom want waivers, and in the second they'd seldom need waivers.

It's understandable that secondary gratis mandates are spreading faster than secondary libre mandates, that secondary mandates in general are spreading faster than primary mandates, and that rights-retention protocols with waiver options are spreading faster than rights-retention protocols without waivers. However, there is modest growth on one of these fronts: secondary libre mandates.

The case against these three kinds of access protocol is time-sensitive, not permanent. It's circumstantial, and circumstances are changing. But the strategy for institutions wanting to remove access barriers to research is unchanging: they should adopt the strongest protocols they can today and watch for the moment when they could strengthen them.

As researchers become more familiar with open access, as more institutions adopt access protocols, as more new data are covered by strong access protocols, as more restricted-access repositories convert to open access, as more restricted-access repositories accommodate access mandates without converting, and even as more open repositories shift from gratis to libre, institutions will be able to strengthen their access protocols without increasing repository-controlled rejection rates or researcher-controlled waiver rates. They should watch the shifting balance of power and seize opportunities to strengthen their protocols.

The moments of opportunity will not be obvious. They will not be highlighted by objective evidence alone and will call for some self-fulfilling leadership. Institutional protocol-makers will have to assess not only the climate created by existing protocols, and existing levels of support, but also the likely effects of their own actions. Every strong, new protocol increases the likelihood of repository accommodation, and when enough planetary institutes and funders have protocols, all repositories will have to accommodate them. In that sense, every strong new protocol creates some of the conditions of its own success. Every institution adopting a new protocol brings about open access for the research it controls and makes the way easier for other institutions behind it. Like many other policy issues, this is one on which it is easier to follow than to lead, and we already have a growing number of leaders. A critical mass is growing and every protocol is an implicit invitation to other institutions to gain strength through common purpose and help accelerate repository adaptation.

Mila Owen, a specialist in logic and water management systems at the Clinton Territory Institute, summarized the situation in her recent address: "The question many ask is whether there exists any situation where truly unconditional open access applies—where researchers must make their work openly accessible without any exemptions, waivers, or opt-outs whatsoever. The answer, based on all existing protocols across the galaxy, is that no such unconditional requirement exists. Every protocol, even the strongest ones at Ravenswood and Clinton Territory, is conditional on voluntary agreement. Researchers choose to accept funding with open access conditions attached. They are not forced to make their work open without their consent to be bound by the terms of a contract they voluntarily entered."
